quests.instruction: Which pair is joined by a nasal sound?
quests.textToSpeak: put it on and leave it
quests.hint: Ask which link would lose its smooth hum if you stopped between the words.
quests.explanation: Put, it, on, and, leave, it: nearly every boundary links, so the sentence is a ribbon of sound. The only nasal link is the /n/ at the end of 'on' running into the weak /ən/ of 'and'; the rest are released stops or a held /v/.
quests.flowRule: Chained links: In phrases like verb + it + particle, each word connects to the next, so one consonant lands on a vowel and the following consonant lands on the next vowel in one flowing line.

quests.instruction: Which link closes the sentence?
quests.textToSpeak: turn it up a little bit
quests.hint: A chain of three links. Take the one that comes last.
quests.explanation: 'Turn it up' is a chain: /n/ onto 'it', /t/ onto 'up', and then the /p/ of 'up' onto the weak /ə/ of 'a'. The last link is the quietest, because 'a' is nearly silent before 'little'.
quests.flowRule: Chained links: In phrases like verb + it + particle, each word connects to the next, so one consonant lands on a vowel and the following consonant lands on the next vowel in one flowing line.

quests.instruction: Find the link carried by the sound /l/
quests.textToSpeak: write it up and email it
quests.hint: Find the word that ends in a dark /l/ and is followed by a vowel.
quests.explanation: The dark /l/ of 'email' stays on the tongue as the vowel of 'it' starts. Everything before it, from 'write it' to 'and email', also links, but through stops and a nasal, so the /l/ link is the only one with a raised tongue.
quests.flowRule: Chained links: In phrases like verb + it + particle, each word connects to the next, so one consonant lands on a vowel and the following consonant lands on the next vowel in one flowing line.

quests.instruction: Find the first place where one word runs into the next
quests.textToSpeak: I just need a name and a number
quests.hint: Count from the start: which link comes earliest?
quests.explanation: The first link is the /d/ of 'need' landing on the weak /ə/ of 'a'. After that, 'name and' and 'and a' keep the line running. Agents say this sentence many times a day, so it often sounds like one long word.
quests.flowRule: Thought groups: Fluent speakers connect words across a whole phrase, so one sentence can contain several links. The instruction tells you which one to find; listen to the sounds on each side of a boundary.

quests.instruction: Find the final link
quests.textToSpeak: we've sent it out and it arrives on Monday
quests.hint: Ignore everything before the last link you hear.
quests.explanation: After 'sent it out and it', the /vz/ of 'arrives' lands on the vowel of 'on'. The final link is easy to lose because 'Monday' carries the stress. Delivery updates are spoken in one rush, so every earlier link feeds into this one.
quests.flowRule: Thought groups: Fluent speakers connect words across a whole phrase, so one sentence can contain several links. The instruction tells you which one to find; listen to the sounds on each side of a boundary.

quests.instruction: Find the link that runs on a hum (m, n or ng)
quests.textToSpeak: that's an easy fix and I'll send it now
quests.hint: Compare the word endings: stops click, hisses buzz, and one ending hums. Which hum is followed by a vowel?
quests.explanation: The weak 'an' hands its /n/ to the stressed vowel of 'easy', and the voice does not stop. 'That's an', 'fix and', 'and I'll' and 'send it' use hisses and stops. A support agent reassuring a customer would say this very smoothly.
quests.flowRule: Consonant-to-Vowel Linking (nasals): A word ending in /m/ or /n/ keeps your voice running, so the nasal sound flows directly into a following vowel with no gap.

quests.instruction: Find the connection that has a link on either side
quests.textToSpeak: Anna will update everyone after the meeting
quests.hint: With three links, the one between the other two is the answer.
quests.explanation: 'Will update', 'update everyone' and 'everyone after' form a chain, and the middle link is the /t/ of 'update' landing on the /e/ of 'everyone'. A meeting-minutes line is read at speed, so you hear it as one phrase.
quests.flowRule: Thought groups: Fluent speakers connect words across a whole phrase, so one sentence can contain several links. The instruction tells you which one to find; listen to the sounds on each side of a boundary.

quests.instruction: Which link is carried by a buzz or a hiss?
quests.textToSpeak: can we move on and discuss costs
quests.hint: Listen for a long /s/, /z/, /f/ or /v/ that slides into a vowel.
quests.explanation: 'Move' ends in /v/, a held sound, and 'on' begins with a vowel, so the airflow keeps going. 'On and' links through /n/ instead. People say this to keep a meeting moving, so it is delivered quickly.
quests.flowRule: Consonant-to-Vowel Linking (continuous sounds): Sounds you can hold, such as /s/, /z/, /f/, /v/ and /ʃ/, glide directly into a following vowel without restarting.

quests.instruction: Only one connection here is real. Which pair?
quests.textToSpeak: can we put one more point on the list
quests.hint: The number word looks as if it could link, but check how it begins. The real link is elsewhere.
quests.explanation: The /t/ of 'point' is released into the vowel of 'on'. 'Put one' looks as if it could link, but 'one' begins with /w/, so it is a consonant meeting a consonant. The other boundaries, such as 'one more', also have a consonant on one side.
quests.flowRule: Thought groups: Fluent speakers connect words across a whole phrase, so one sentence can contain several links. The instruction tells you which one to find; listen to the sounds on each side of a boundary.

quests.instruction: Which pair is joined by an -ed ending?
quests.textToSpeak: I've worked at several banks and an insurance company
quests.hint: Which verb ends in a past-tense -ed that you might be tempted to drop?
quests.explanation: The -ed of 'worked' is /t/ and it lands on the weak /ət/ of 'at'. The rest of the sentence, 'banks and', 'and an' and 'an insurance', links through other sounds. Keeping that /t/ is what tells the interviewer it is past experience.
quests.flowRule: Past-tense endings link too: A final -ed (/t/ or /d/) joins a following vowel, which also keeps the past-tense signal audible.

quests.instruction: Which pair is joined by a 'th' sound?
quests.textToSpeak: most days I work with an international team
quests.hint: Tongue between the teeth: find the word that ends that way and is followed by a vowel.
quests.explanation: The /ð/ at the end of 'with' flows into the weak /ən/ of 'an', and then straight on into 'international'. The first link, 'days I', uses /z/, so the 'th' link is the only one carried by a 'th' sound.
quests.flowRule: Consonant-to-Vowel Linking (/θ/ and /ð/): The 'th' sounds at the end of a word stay in the airflow and connect to a following vowel instead of stopping.

quests.instruction: Count the links from the start: find the second one
quests.textToSpeak: the project I led at university went really well
quests.hint: Listen for the second join, not the first.
quests.explanation: 'Project I' and 'led at' both link. The second is the /d/ of 'led' landing on the weak /æt/ of 'at', right before 'university' begins with /j/, which is a consonant sound. In an interview answer, links keep a long sentence from sounding like a list.
quests.flowRule: Thought groups: Fluent speakers connect words across a whole phrase, so one sentence can contain several links. The instruction tells you which one to find; listen to the sounds on each side of a boundary.

quests.instruction: Which link carries the past-tense ending?
quests.textToSpeak: we booked an extra night online
quests.hint: Listen for the small /t/ or /d/ at the end of a past verb, joined to the next vowel.
quests.explanation: 'Booked' ends in /kt/, and the /t/ lands on the weak /ən/ of 'an'. Without that /t/ you would hear the present tense. 'An extra' and 'night online' link too, but they carry no grammar.
quests.flowRule: Past-tense endings link too: A final -ed (/t/ or /d/) joins a following vowel, which also keeps the past-tense signal audible.

quests.instruction: Find the link into a word whose h you do not pronounce
quests.textToSpeak: the shuttle runs every half hour
quests.hint: One word begins with a letter you do not pronounce. Which?
quests.explanation: In 'hour' the h is silent, so the word begins with a vowel and 'half' can link straight into it. 'Runs every' also links, but only 'half hour' depends on a silent letter.
quests.flowRule: Silent 'h': In words like 'hour', 'honest' and 'honour' the written h is not pronounced, so the word begins with a vowel sound and links to the word before it (and takes 'an', not 'a').

quests.instruction: Find the link that keeps a past-tense -ed audible
quests.textToSpeak: is breakfast included in the price
quests.hint: The past-tense ending matters for meaning. Which boundary carries it?
quests.explanation: 'Included' ends in /d/ and 'in' begins with a vowel, so the voice runs on, and the /d/ also keeps the participle clear. 'Breakfast included' links through /t/. Hotel guests ask this fast, so the chain runs in one breath.
quests.flowRule: Past-tense endings link too: A final -ed (/t/ or /d/) joins a following vowel, which also keeps the past-tense signal audible.

quests.instruction: Which link has a nasal sound meeting a vowel?
quests.textToSpeak: she had a salad and an apple
quests.hint: Imagine saying 'mm' or 'nn' between the two words. Which boundary already contains one?
quests.explanation: 'An' ends in /n/ and 'apple' begins with /æ/, so the voice carries on. 'Had a', 'salad and' and 'and an' link through /d/. The sentence builds toward its last link, which is the only nasal one.
quests.flowRule: Consonant-to-Vowel Linking (nasals): A word ending in /m/ or /n/ keeps your voice running, so the nasal sound flows directly into a following vowel with no gap.

quests.instruction: Which connection comes first in this sentence?
quests.textToSpeak: the kitchen closes at ten and opens again at six
quests.hint: A long sentence with five links. Take the first.
quests.explanation: 'Closes' ends in /z/ and 'at' is the weak /ət/, so the first link is the voiced hiss running on. The rest, 'ten and', 'and opens', 'opens again' and 'again at', follow in a chain. A restaurant sign read aloud sounds like this.
quests.flowRule: Thought groups: Fluent speakers connect words across a whole phrase, so one sentence can contain several links. The instruction tells you which one to find; listen to the sounds on each side of a boundary.

quests.instruction: Which pair is joined by an -ed ending?
quests.textToSpeak: we waited almost an hour
quests.hint: Past-tense endings often sound like /t/, /d/ or /ɪd/. Which one meets a vowel?
quests.explanation: 'Waited' ends in /ɪd/, and its /d/ runs into the /ɔː/ of 'almost'. 'Almost an' and 'an hour' follow. Dropping the /d/ would blur the tense, so linking is what keeps it clear.
quests.flowRule: Past-tense endings link too: A final -ed (/t/ or /d/) joins a following vowel, which also keeps the past-tense signal audible.

quests.instruction: Find the link where a held sound like s, z, f or v flows into a vowel
quests.textToSpeak: I've had a sore throat and a cough all week
quests.hint: One boundary flows like air through a gap. Which?
quests.explanation: 'Cough' ends in /f/, which you can hold, and 'all' begins with a vowel, so the hiss runs on. 'Had a', 'throat and' and 'and a' are carried by stops, so they are released rather than held.
quests.flowRule: Consonant-to-Vowel Linking (continuous sounds): Sounds you can hold, such as /s/, /z/, /f/, /v/ and /ʃ/, glide directly into a following vowel without restarting.

quests.instruction: Which link carries the past-tense ending?
quests.textToSpeak: the pharmacist checked if I'm allergic
quests.hint: Without that final sound, one verb would sound present tense. Which?
quests.explanation: The -ed of 'checked' is a /t/ that lands on the vowel of 'if'. 'Pharmacist checked' does not link, because /t/ meets /tʃ/. 'If I'm' and 'I'm allergic' follow, so the whole sentence is a chain.
quests.flowRule: Past-tense endings link too: A final -ed (/t/ or /d/) joins a following vowel, which also keeps the past-tense signal audible.

quests.instruction: Which link do you hear first?
quests.textToSpeak: you should rest and drink a lot of water
quests.hint: Listen from the beginning. The first link is the one the question wants.
quests.explanation: 'Rest' ends in /st/, and the /t/ (or just the /s/ in fast speech) lands on the weak /ən/ of 'and'. 'Drink a' and 'lot of' follow. Medical advice is often given as one fluent phrase, and the cluster makes this first link the hardest to hear.
quests.flowRule: Linking after consonant clusters: When a word ends in two or three consonants, the last one still connects into a following vowel, so the ending is carried across the boundary smoothly.

quests.instruction: Which is the last connection in this sentence?
quests.textToSpeak: chop an onion and add it to the pan
quests.hint: Say the sentence and keep going until the last join. Which one is it?
quests.explanation: The chain 'chop an onion and add it' links all the way: /p/ onto 'an', /n/ onto 'onion', /n/ onto 'and', /d/ onto 'add', /d/ onto 'it'. The last link is the final /d/ landing on the weak 'it', and the stress falls on 'pan'.
quests.flowRule: Chained links: In phrases like verb + it + particle, each word connects to the next, so one consonant lands on a vowel and the following consonant lands on the next vowel in one flowing line.

quests.instruction: Which link sits in the middle of the sentence?
quests.textToSpeak: insert the plug and turn it on
quests.hint: Find the link that has a link on both sides of it.
quests.explanation: 'Plug and', 'turn it' and 'it on' form a short run. The middle link is the /n/ of 'turn' onto the weak 'it', right before 'on'. Instructions are spoken in rhythm, so the chain makes a pattern.
quests.flowRule: Chained links: In phrases like verb + it + particle, each word connects to the next, so one consonant lands on a vowel and the following consonant lands on the next vowel in one flowing line.

quests.instruction: Which pair is joined by an /l/?
quests.textToSpeak: mix it well and let it cool
quests.hint: The tongue stays on the ridge behind the teeth as the next vowel begins. Where?
quests.explanation: The dark /l/ of 'well' stays on the tongue as the weak /ən/ of 'and' begins. 'Mix it' and 'let it' use /ks/ and /t/. In a recipe, this link sits right between two instructions, and a pause would split them.
quests.flowRule: Consonant-to-Vowel Linking (/l/): A word-final /l/ stays voiced and slides into the vowel of the next word, so the two words sound like one continuous stretch.

quests.instruction: Find the link carried by the sound /l/
quests.textToSpeak: a couple of eggs and a bit of cheese
quests.hint: Of all the endings, one is made with the tongue tip raised. Which word is it?
quests.explanation: 'Couple' ends in a syllabic /l/ and 'of' is the weak /əv/, so the tongue stays up while the vowel starts. 'Of eggs', 'eggs and', 'and a' and 'bit of' follow. Quantity phrases are among the most reduced in English.
quests.flowRule: Reduced forms: Unstressed to, and, of, at, it, us and a shrink to /tə/, /ən/, /əv/, /ət/, /ɪt/, /əs/ and /ə/, so a link into one of them sounds like the end of the word before it.

quests.instruction: Which pair is joined by a nasal sound?
quests.textToSpeak: we sort of ran out of time
quests.hint: One boundary keeps the voice running without any burst or hiss. Where?
quests.explanation: The /n/ of 'ran' runs into the /aʊ/ of 'out'. 'Sort of' and 'out of' link through /t/. 'Sort of' often reduces to 'sorta', and the overall rhythm leans on 'ran out'.
quests.flowRule: Consonant-to-Vowel Linking (nasals): A word ending in /m/ or /n/ keeps your voice running, so the nasal sound flows directly into a following vowel with no gap.

quests.instruction: Which link closes the sentence?
quests.textToSpeak: we'll sort it out and let you know
quests.hint: Work backwards from the end of the sentence.
quests.explanation: 'Sort it', 'it out' and 'out and' form a chain, and the last link is the /t/ of 'out' landing on the weak /ən/. Agents promise action in one breath, so you hear one flowing phrase.
quests.flowRule: Reduced forms: Unstressed to, and, of, at, it, us and a shrink to /tə/, /ən/, /əv/, /ət/, /ɪt/, /əs/ and /ə/, so a link into one of them sounds like the end of the word before it.

quests.instruction: Find the link that runs on a hum (m, n or ng)
quests.textToSpeak: let's meet around ten and ask everyone
quests.hint: In which pair does the first word end with your mouth closed or your tongue tip up, with sound still flowing?
quests.explanation: The /n/ of 'ten' flows into the weak /ən/ of 'and'. The rest of the chain, 'meet around', 'and ask' and 'ask everyone', uses stops. A quick plan like this is said in one breath.
quests.flowRule: Consonant-to-Vowel Linking (nasals): A word ending in /m/ or /n/ keeps your voice running, so the nasal sound flows directly into a following vowel with no gap.

quests.instruction: Find the final link
quests.textToSpeak: he's out of office until Monday
quests.hint: The answer sits closer to the end than the start. Which link is it?
quests.explanation: The /s/ of 'office' lands on the /ʌ/ of 'until', and the stress falls on 'Mon'. 'He's out', 'out of' and 'of office' form the chain before it. An out-of-office message is typically read in a fast, flat tone.
quests.flowRule: Thought groups: Fluent speakers connect words across a whole phrase, so one sentence can contain several links. The instruction tells you which one to find; listen to the sounds on each side of a boundary.

quests.instruction: Which link goes into a word with a silent h?
quests.textToSpeak: she gave an honest answer
quests.hint: Check the spelling of the words after the link: one starts with an h that is silent.
quests.explanation: 'Honest' begins with a vowel because the h is silent, so 'an' runs straight into it. 'Gave an' and 'honest answer' also link, but only the middle link depends on a silent letter.
quests.flowRule: Silent 'h': In words like 'hour', 'honest' and 'honour' the written h is not pronounced, so the word begins with a vowel sound and links to the word before it (and takes 'an', not 'a').
